chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
title: An eight-hundred-mile drive and Armstrong playing hard regardless
summary: A Chicago-to-engagement run turned out to be eight hundred miles, and Armstrong still blew everyone off the stand on arrival.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: So as soon as you finished the job, into the bus and...

Into the bus, and four hundred more miles, or five or six or seven or eight hundred miles. We left Chicago one morning, we thought we was going six hundred miles to the next engagement. And when we got on the road and the road manager looked at the contract, we found out it was eight hundred miles instead of six hundred miles. And we had left Chicago...oh, it was after three o'clock in the morning when we left there, and we were due at this next engagement... This was eight hundred miles. We were due on the bandstand at eight o'clock, or else there would have been a big fine for being late -- stipulated on the contract. So this fellow, boy, he drove that bus, too. Oh. He didn't stop for nothin'. At eight o'clock was on the bandstand. We were damn near dead, though. But we was on the bandstand.
And you had only one driver?
He did the whole thing. We didn't even

stop for nothin'. And we went on the bandstand. Of course, everybody was dead tired. Louis got up there and blew like he had been sleepin' in a Pullman berth or something. He blew his head off. I said, "This man is...he's too great. Everybody else is..." I couldn't keep my eyes open, I was so damn tired and sleepy. And just blew and blew. I mean, he played... And I said, "No, this is too hard. This is too hard." He said, "Well, you blow out the bad ones like you blow out the good ones. Blow 'em loud." Oh, he liked you to blow loud.

Yeah, he was a hard worker. He was a hard workin' man. He worked hard. There was nothin'... Now we had traveled eight hundred miles, you know, you'd get out, you can't hardly stand up, and you'd think he would take it easy the first few sets or something like that. No-o. No. He got on there that first number, boy, and pound-pound-pound. Well, the house was full of people. And there was no let-up. He was there to entertain the people, and believe me, that's what he believed in. People pay their money, they don't care what you go through. They paid their admission. They want to be entertained. He was absolutely right. Your feelings meant nothin'.
Yessir, he was a hard worker and a hard-workin' man, and he didn't ask you to do nothin' that he wouldn't do.
He played, and played hard. That's why I say he was a great man, because no other leader I know would have put up with what he had to go through.
